digest.title: Material Intelligence — October 12, 2026
digest.description: An entirely AI-generated weekly digest of AI for materials science, based only on supplied source records.
digest.overview: This week's eight selections highlight pressure-transferable potentials, leaner training datasets, diffraction-to-structure models, and AI-guided materials screening. A recurring theme is that benchmark success depends on the reference physics and chemical environments represented in training. All selected sources are preprints available here only as abstracts; computational predictions are not evidence of successful synthesis or experimental performance.

stories.title: A high-pressure benchmark exposes gaps in universal potentials
stories.summary: The WBM-MatPES preprint introduces 182,000 consistently recomputed structures, reference convex hulls, and tests at six pressures up to 150 GPa. Five published MatPES potentials agree within 12 meV/atom at 25 GPa, but their errors rise to 0.4–5 eV/atom at 150 GPa. The authors' Tuga-FF graph transformer reports energy errors of 13.6 meV/atom at ambient pressure and 21 meV/atom at 150 GPa.
stories.whyItMatters: Pressure is a concrete test of whether a potential transfers beyond familiar configurations. Pairing a benchmark with pressure-diverse training offers a practical route to more reliable high-pressure screening rather than assuming that an ambient-pressure model remains accurate under compression.
stories.limitation: These are computational comparisons at the benchmark's chosen level of electronic-structure theory, not experimental validation. The abstract does not establish performance beyond the tested chemistry and pressure range, or independent reproduction of Tuga-FF's reported advantage.

sources.title: Pressure-transferable universal machine-learning potentials: the WBM-MatPES benchmark and Tuga-FF
sources.evidence: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials hold the promise to replace costly ab initio calculations in materials science workflows. However, the accuracy and transferability of current models are limited by the availability of training data. We release WBM-MatPES, a dataset of 182 thousand structures recomputed with consistent MatPES settings, together with two reference convex hulls of different depths and test sets at six pressures up to 150 GPa. These datasets reproduce a realistic discovery workflow and allow potentials to be ranked systematically at this level of theory, similar to the Matbench Discovery leaderboard at the Materials Project settings. In this benchmark, five published MatPES potentials agree within 12 meV/atom at 25 GPa, yet their errors increase dramatically to 0.4-5 eV/atom at 150 GPa. To address this limitation, we develop Tuga-FF, a graph transformer trained on datasets spanning ambient and high-pressure configurations alike. Tuga-FF is the most accurate model in the benchmark at ambient pressure, with an energy error of 13.6 meV/atom, and maintains an error of just 21 meV/atom at 150 GPa. We believe this benchmark will encourage the community to train higher-accuracy models and generate richer datasets, advancing machine-learned interatomic potentials as a whole.

stories.title: Small OMat24 subsets challenge the case for ever-larger training sets
stories.summary: A preprint trains MACE models on subsets containing 6.5 million atoms, described as less than 1% of OMat24, selected randomly, through latent-space clustering, or with the new local-environment method EnvTok. The resulting models approach the full-data reference in force accuracy and remain close to or exceed it on several property and simulation tests.
stories.whyItMatters: If diverse local environments carry most of the useful information, dataset construction could prioritize coverage over repeated configurations. EnvTok selects environments before labeling or training, potentially freeing expensive reference-calculation budgets for higher-level theory or underrepresented chemistry.
stories.limitation: The headline claim of 99% redundancy is supported here by particular OMat24 subsets, MACE models, and reported tests—not every materials dataset or architecture. Similar performance across all three selection strategies also means these results do not establish a unique predictive advantage for EnvTok.

sources.title: Atoms that Matter: Largest Materials Datasets Are 99% Redundant, and Local Chemistry Can Guide the Required 1%
sources.evidence: General-purpose machine-learning force fields (MLFFs) for materials are now trained on the order of $100$ million structures, assuming transferability requires such scale. We test this premise on OMat24, the largest available materials dataset, by training MACE models on subsets of $6.5$ million atoms, less than $1\%$ of OMat24, selected in three complementary ways: at random, by latent-space clustering of a pretrained MLFF (DIRECT), and by a new model-free method maximizing the diversity of discrete, interpretable local environments (EnvTok). All three models approach the full-data reference MACE-OMAT-0 model to within a few tens of $\mathrm{meV}/\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ in forces, and remain close to or exceed it on formation energies, elastic moduli, heat capacities, Li$^{+}$ migration barriers, and molecular-dynamics stability up to $3000\,$K and $500\,$GPa. This near-independence from the selection strategy shows that chemical environment diversity, not size, defines OMat24's information content: the remaining $99\%$ of structures are largely redundant. Broad sampling of chemical space thus remains essential, but reference labels are needed only for structurally and chemically distinct configurations. Using atomic positions and species, optionally augmented by magnetic moments, EnvTok identifies these before any labelling or training, yielding compact, architecture-independent datasets. This hundredfold reduction makes hybrid-DFT or higher-level relabelling of general-purpose training sets feasible, and frees computational budget for extending environmental coverage and multi-fidelity learning.

stories.title: PXRD-Bench tests structure recovery beyond idealized powder patterns
stories.summary: PXRD-Bench introduces approximately 4.1 million training structures with simulated powder X-ray diffraction, plus evaluations involving unseen compositions, unseen structural prototypes, unknown per-element atom counts, and two-phase mixtures. Its Bragglite baseline reports a 44.2% Top-1 structure-match rate on experimental RRUFF patterns when composition is known.
stories.whyItMatters: A shared benchmark can reveal whether diffraction-to-structure models handle conditions closer to materials characterization rather than only clean, single-phase simulated inputs. Experimental-pattern evaluation excludes structurally matching training entries, addressing an important route to misleadingly strong results.
stories.limitation: This preprint's strongest quoted result still assumes known composition and leaves most patterns without a correct Top-1 match. Unseen prototypes and two-phase recovery remain difficult; the abstract does not demonstrate routine structure solution for arbitrary experimental samples.

sources.title: PXRD-Bench: How Close Are We to Determining Crystal Structures from Powder Diffraction?
sources.evidence: Determining crystal structures from powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) would enable routine characterization of newly synthesized materials, including those absent from reference databases. Generative models offer a promising approach, but existing evaluations remain fragmented and largely assume single-phase samples with known composition. To fill this gap, we introduce PXRD-Bench, a unified benchmark that extends evaluation to unknown per-element atom counts and recovery of both structures in two-phase mixtures. It provides approximately 4.1 million training structures with simulated PXRD, tests generalization to unseen compositions and structural prototypes, and evaluates recovery from experimental PXRD after excluding structurally matching training entries. To provide a strong reference baseline, we also introduce Bragglite, a PXRD-to-structure model developed through a systematic study of PXRD modeling choices. It achieves a 44.2\% Top-1 match rate on experimental RRUFF patterns with known composition, 24.6\% above the strongest prior baseline. Further analysis yields several key findings: some models fail to benefit from experimental PXRD, while generalization to unseen structural prototypes and recovery from two-phase mixtures remain challenging. Together, our benchmark, systematic studies, and Bragglite clarify the capabilities and limitations of current PXRD-to-structure models.

stories.title: DiffGA steers a frozen crystal generator with evolutionary search
stories.summary: DiffGA combines evolutionary search during diffusion sampling with a frozen MatterGen backbone and an on-the-fly Bayesian surrogate using force-field graph embeddings. Across three crystal-design tasks, the preprint reports better oracle-assessed rates of stable, unique, and novel hits than several baselines, including compute-matched alternatives. Selected hits undergo first-principles reevaluation.
stories.whyItMatters: Retraining-free steering could make generative design more adaptable when objectives change or cannot supply gradients. Reusing evaluations through a surrogate targets a central campaign expense: repeatedly calculating candidate properties.
stories.limitation: The authors present a method evaluation rather than experimentally discovered compounds. They identify systematic bias in machine-learned force-field oracles in some regimes, and first-principles checking of a representative sample does not validate every generated hit or establish synthesizability.

sources.title: DiffGA: Steering Frozen Diffusion Models for Materials Design via Evolutionary Search
sources.evidence: Steering candidate generation toward user-defined objectives is central to inverse materials design, yet remains difficult when objectives are black-box, changing, or non-differentiable, as in many simulation- and experiment-derived properties. Generative models offer a solution but typically require retraining or fine-tuning for each new objective, demanding labeled data and substantial compute, or rely on differentiable guidance that is brittle to gradient noise and undefined for many practical targets. We present DiffGA, a retraining-free framework that injects evolutionary search into the sampling trajectory of a retrained diffusion model, evolving partially denoised states under an arbitrary black-box oracle. Because oracle evaluation often dominates campaign cost, we couple DiffGA with an on-the-fly Bayesian surrogate that reuses representations from state-of-the-art machine-learned force fields (MLFFs). A Gaussian process is fit during the campaign on the force fields's graph embeddings and, once it demonstrably ranks an unseen generation, replaces expensive property evaluations under an uncertainty-aware acquisition rule, reducing oracle cost with negligible loss of accuracy. Across three crystal-design tasks using a frozen MatterGen backbone, DiffGA outperforms diffusion-only, compute-matched, purely evolutionary, and fine-tuned baselines in oracle-assessed rates of stable, unique, and novel hits. Rather than proposing scientific compounds, we use density functional theory to quantify MLFF oracle fidelity, showing that it is a faithful proxy in key regimes but systematically biased in others, delineating when proxy-driven generative discovery can be trusted. On a representative sample, DiffGA's top hits survive first principles re-evaluation as physically realistic hits, while the surrogate-accelerated pipeline preserves this fidelity at a fraction of the cost.

stories.title: Inverse design predicts two strongly polar Bi2O3 monolayers
stories.summary: An inverse-design workflow combining a machine-learning interatomic potential and first-principles calculations identifies previously unreported tetragonal and orthorhombic Bi2O3 monolayers. Calculated out-of-plane two-dimensional polarizations are 34.12 and 37.15 pC/m. The preprint also reports dynamical stability, finite-temperature structural integrity, and band gaps near 3.8 eV.
stories.whyItMatters: The study suggests that reconstructing nonlayered oxide networks into two dimensions can create strong intrinsic polarity. That provides a design motif for screening polar oxides beyond familiar layered structures, with possible relevance to nanoscale electronics and surface-charge control.
stories.limitation: Both monolayers and their properties are computational predictions, not synthesized materials or measured devices. Simulated stability does not establish a practical growth route, substrate compatibility, long-term stability, or electrically switchable ferroelectric behavior.

sources.title: Large Out-of-plane Polarization in Two-dimensional Bi2O3 Monolayers Predicted by an AI-driven Inverse-design Workflow
sources.evidence: Two-dimensional (2D) polar oxides with built-in electric fields offer promising opportunities for nanoscale electronics, optoelectronics, and surface charge engineering. However, their discovery remains challenging due to the enormous structural complexity of nonlayered oxide networks. Here, we combine inverse structural design with a machine-learning interatomic potential and first-principles calculations to explore 2D oxide configurations. Using Bi2O3 as a representative system, we identify two previously unreported polar monolayers with tetragonal and orthorhombic symmetries. Both structures exhibit vertically separated Bi and O sublayers, giving rise to pronounced intrinsic polarity with Berry-phase 2D polarizations of 34.12 and 37.15 pC/m, respectively. Notably, the o-Bi2O3 monolayer exhibits one of the largest reported out-of-plane polarizations among 2D oxides. Both monolayers exhibit dynamical stability, finite-temperature structural integrity, and wide band gaps (~3.8 eV). The large polarization originates from dimensionality-induced reconstruction of the nonlayered Bi-O network, which breaks local coordination symmetry and produces out-of-plane charge redistribution, while the stereochemically active Bi 6s2 lone pair further favors asymmetric Bi-O bonding. These findings suggest dimensionality-induced local-coordination symmetry breaking as a promising design motif for high-polarization 2D oxides, and demonstrate the utility of combining inverse design with machine-learning-assisted screening to explore unconventional polar phases in nonlayered oxide networks.

stories.title: Small polarons reveal an electronic blind spot in universal potentials
stories.summary: A geometry-based benchmark examines hydrogen-induced electron localization in transition-metal oxides using metal–oxygen bond expansion as a descriptor. Universal potentials show behavior ranging from delocalized states to metastable small polarons. Although some reproduce hopping barriers, all tested models fail to stabilize spatially separated polaron–donor configurations, favoring localization near hydrogen instead.
stories.whyItMatters: Accurate atomic forces alone may not guarantee reliable charge-localization physics. For oxide transport, catalysis, and degradation studies, this benchmark makes the treatment of electronic correlations and the contents of reference training data explicit model-selection concerns.
stories.limitation: This preprint uses geometry as a proxy for localization and compares against DFT+U predictions, rather than directly demonstrating experimental electronic states. Its findings concern the tested models and hydrogen-induced configurations, not a proof that all future potentials must fail.

sources.title: Can Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Capture Small Polarons? A Geometry-Based Benchmark in Transition-Metal Oxides
sources.evidence: Small polarons, formed when excess electrons become localized through lattice distortions, play a critical role in charge transport, catalysis, and degradation processes in transition-metal (TM) oxides. Whether universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs), which lack explicit electronic degrees of freedom, can describe them remains unclear. Here, we investigate H-induced electron localization across a range of TM oxides using a geometric descriptor based on TM-O bond-length expansion (Z-score) to identify polaronic distortions. We find that uMLIPs exhibit varying degrees of electron localization, from delocalized states to metastable small polarons, with their behavior strongly dependent on the training data and treatment of electronic correlations. In particular, the absence of Hubbard U corrections for specific TM cations in the training data leads to electron delocalization, in contrast to DFT+U predictions. Although some uMLIPs reproduce polaron hopping barriers during coupled proton-polaron transfer, all of them fail to stabilize spatially separated polaron-donor configurations, instead favoring localization near the H dopant.

stories.title: A neural potential brings SrTiO3 vacancy transport closer to experiment
stories.summary: Researchers train a neural network potential on first-principles molecular-dynamics data for pristine and oxygen-deficient SrTiO3, then use longer and larger simulations to study vacancy diffusion. The preprint reports a migration enthalpy of 0.64 eV, compared with a cited experimental value of 0.67 eV, and better diffusion-coefficient agreement than conventional classical molecular dynamics.
stories.whyItMatters: Defect transport often requires trajectories beyond practical direct first-principles simulation. This result illustrates how a targeted potential can connect electronic-structure reference calculations to longer-timescale transport observables while retaining a quantitative experimental comparison.
stories.limitation: The reported migration enthalpy is a simulation result compared with experimental data, not a new experimental measurement. Agreement for the reported vacancy problem does not establish accuracy across other defect species, concentrations, charge states, or operating conditions.

sources.title: Theoretical Investigation of Oxygen-Vacancy Diffusion in SrTiO$_3$ using Neural Network Potentials
sources.evidence: Oxygen-vacancy formation and diffusion play important roles in determining the electronic and atomic transport properties of SrTiO$_3$ (STO). Accurate analysis of such point defects requires sufficiently large-scale and long-time molecular dynamics (MD) simulations; however, direct investigations of oxygen-vacancy dynamics using {\it ab initio} MD (AIMD) based on density functional theory (DFT) are limited to relatively small systems and short time scales because of their high computational cost. In this study, we develop a neural network potential (NNP) for pristine and oxygen-deficient STO using a reference dataset generated from AIMD simulations. The trained NNP model accurately reproduces the DFT reference energies, atomic forces, and virials for both pristine STO and STO containing an oxygen vacancy. The NNP also reproduces the supercell-size dependence of the total energies and oxygen-vacancy formation energies, including the formation energy extrapolated to the dilute limit. Large-scale and long-time MD simulations using the NNP (NNP-MD) are then performed to investigate oxygen-vacancy diffusion. The resulting oxygen-vacancy diffusion coefficients show substantially better agreement with experimental data than those obtained from conventional classical MD simulations. An Arrhenius analysis yields an oxygen-vacancy migration enthalpy of 0.64 eV, in close agreement with the experimental value of 0.67 eV. These results demonstrate that NNPs trained on first-principles data provide an accurate and computationally efficient framework for investigating defect formation and long-time vacancy transport in perovskite oxides.

stories.title: Graph-based screening improves predicted methanol yields for doped zirconia
stories.summary: An extended Wasserstein Weisfeiler–Lehman Gaussian-process model predicts adsorption and transition-state energies on ZrO2 surfaces doped with Al, Cd, Ga, In, or Zn. The preprint reports improved intermediate-energy predictions over thermodynamic scaling relations and competitive transition-state estimates. Propagating those energies through microkinetics yields methanol predictions closer to DFT-derived results than the linear-relation workflow.
stories.whyItMatters: Catalyst screening needs errors assessed at the reaction-network level, not only as isolated energy metrics. Connecting graph predictions to methanol yield and rate-controlling steps shows where a surrogate's improvements could materially change candidate rankings.
stories.limitation: The yield comparison is between computational workflows using DFT-derived references, not measured catalytic production. The supplied abstract gives no quantitative yield-error reduction, and evidence is limited to the specified dopants, surface, and reaction network.

sources.title: Improved screening of doped ZrO$_2$ catalysts for CO$_2$ hydrogenation from graph-based machine learning
sources.evidence: Dopants can tune the activity of zirconia-based CO$_2$ hydrogenation catalysts through changes in adsorbate and transition-state (TS) energetics. Computing these quantities with density functional theory (DFT) becomes expensive when several dopants, reaction intermediates, and TSs must be screened. Here, we further develop the graph-based machine learning method Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman Gaussian Process Regression (WWL-GPR): we introduce additional electronic-structure and local-environment features relevant for oxide surfaces and use the resulting model to predict adsorption and TS energies on ZrO$_2$(101) surfaces doped with Al$^{3+}$, Cd$^{2+}$, Ga$^{3+}$, In$^{3+}$, and Zn$^{2+}$. Adsorbate-surface structures are represented as attributed graphs that combine bonds connectivity and features. We benchmark WWL-GPR against thermodynamic scaling relations (TSR) for reaction intermediates and Bronsted-Evans-Polanyi relations (BEP) for TSs, and then propagate the predicted energies to microkinetic CH$_3$OH-yield estimates. WWL-GPR consistently improves the prediction of reaction intermediate energetics relative to linear scaling approaches and provides TS estimates that are competitive with BEP-based models. These improvements become especially relevant when the predicted energetics are propagated through the reaction network. Microkinetic calculations show that WWL-GPR-derived energies give CH$_3$OH yields closer to DFT-derived yields than the linear-relation workflow. Degree-of-rate-control analysis links the activity errors to dopant-dependent rate-controlling steps, including HCOO* formation, H$_2$COOH* dissociation, and H$_3$CO* formation. These results support WWL-GPR as a data-efficient surrogate for connecting atomistic energetics with catalyst-screening observables on doped oxide surfaces.
